lesson_title: One Pair of Shoes, Followed All the Way: Manufacturing Cost Accounting
hook_text: What does ONE school shoe actually cost to make? Follow the rand and find out.
clip_script: You are frying vetkoek for the school fete — five hundred of them. What does ONE cost? Start sorting and you are doing cost accounting. Flour, oil, mince — you can point at them inside the vetkoek: direct materials. Your cousin frying all day for a fee: direct labour. Together, prime cost — everything that touches the product. But the stand also burned gas, hired a gazebo, wore out a borrowed fryer. Nothing sits inside any one vetkoek, yet without it there is no frying: that basket is overheads. And the flyers you printed? Selling cost — cost of the day, not of the vetkoek. Keep it out, or the unit cost lies. Now scale up to a shoe factory: leather issued to the floor, R538 000. Machinists' wages, R402 000. Overheads basket, R400 000. Out come 24 000 finished pairs costing R1 320 000 — fifty-five rand a pair. That number is the factory's heartbeat. Price at eighty and you know, before selling one shoe, what is there for the office, the deliveries and the profit. Watch fifty-five drift upward, and you know the floor is leaking before any statement says so. One rand, one path: sacks, floor, store, customer.
visual_style: A sizzling fete stand morphing into a factory floor, costs riding conveyor belts through four labelled stations, a glowing unit-cost heartbeat monitor; warm KwaZulu-Natal workshop palette with leather and chalk textures.
pacing: Playful vetkoek sort, then a driving conveyor sequence to the heartbeat reveal.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and walk the rand's whole path yourself.
